 New Jersey REAL ID appointment wait times drop from 73 days to just three days 
 Jay Edwards November 10, 2026 75 3 minutes read 
 NEW JERSEY — New Jersey residents preparing for holiday travel can now schedule REAL ID appointments with an average wait of just three days, down from 73 days at the beginning of 2026, according to the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission.
 With Thanksgiving approaching, state officials are encouraging residents who need a REAL ID to schedule appointments while availability remains high at NJMVC agencies across the state. 
 The improvement represents a 96% reduction in appointment wait times following operational changes implemented by the Sherrill administration. The NJMVC has issued approximately 750,000 REAL IDs in 2026 and is approaching 1 million for the year, according to state officials.
 “Government should make people’s lives easier,” said Governor Sherrill. “New Jerseyans were waiting an average of 73 days for a REAL ID appointment, and that was unacceptable. We made operational improvements at the MVC, and now residents can get an appointment in just three days as they prepare for holiday travel.”
 Acting NJMVC Chief Administrator Rosalie Johnson said the agency has made significant progress in improving access to REAL ID appointments.
 “We’ve made REAL ID appointments more accessible and convenient than ever before,” said Acting NJMVC Chief Administrator Rosalie Johnson. “Back in January, New Jersey residents were waiting, on average, over two months to get an appointment. Today, you can schedule an appointment online in minutes and be serviced within days. We’ve cut appointment wait times by 96 percent. This is the kind of progress that New Jerseyans deserve.”
 REAL ID requirements for air travel 
 Since May 2025, the Transportation Security Administration has required travelers 18 and older to present a REAL ID-compliant driver’s license or another acceptable form of identification to board domestic commercial flights.
 Standard New Jersey driver’s licenses and identification cards without the REAL ID star symbol are no longer accepted as identification at TSA airport security checkpoints.
 However, residents with a valid U.S. passport, passport card, military identification or another TSA-approved form of identification do not need a REAL ID to fly domestically.
 REAL ID-compliant identification can also be used to enter certain federal facilities.
 Changes that reduced appointment wait times 
 According to the NJMVC, the reduction in wait times was achieved through operational improvements rather than increased spending.
 One significant change allows residents to present electronic proof of residency, including bank statements, utility bills and pay stubs, directly from a smartphone or tablet instead of providing paper copies.
 The agency said accepting digital documents has reduced failed transactions and repeat customer visits by half at NJMVC locations statewide.
 The NJMVC also streamlined document verification procedures and expanded acceptable documentation options, allowing employees to process transactions more efficiently while maintaining security standards.
 Additionally, operational improvements enabled the agency to increase appointment availability statewide and expand REAL ID services to seven additional agencies in 2026.
 “We solved capacity challenges by working smarter, not spending more,” added Acting Chief Administrator Johnson. “These targeted changes are proof government can deliver better results through creative thinking and improved operations.”
 How to obtain a REAL ID in New Jersey 
 Residents seeking a REAL ID must provide several documents to establish their identity, Social Security number and New Jersey residency.
 The NJMVC requires:
 Two proofs of New Jersey residency: Acceptable documents include utility bills, bank statements, mortgages and leases. Residency documents may be presented on paper or electronically using a smartphone or tablet.
 A valid Social Security number: The number will be verified through the Social Security Administration. If verification fails, applicants must provide additional documentation, such as a Social Security card, W-2 form or pay stub showing their full Social Security number.
 Proof of identity: Applicants must provide primary and secondary identification documents totaling six REAL ID points. Examples include a valid U.S. passport or certified birth certificate. Identity documents must be original paper documents or certified copies.
 Residents are encouraged to review the NJMVC’s online REAL ID checklist and document selector before scheduling an appointment to ensure they have the required paperwork.
 Appointments can be scheduled through the NJMVC’s online appointment system. Residents whose driver’s license or identification card expires within three months may also upgrade to a REAL ID during a renewal appointment.
 At the appointment, NJMVC employees will verify the required documents, take the applicant’s photograph and issue a temporary paper license.
 The fee is $35 for a four-year REAL ID driver’s license or identification card. Residents upgrading before their renewal window while keeping their existing expiration date will pay $11.
 The permanent REAL ID will be mailed to the applicant within approximately two weeks.
 State officials are encouraging residents to schedule appointments ahead of the holiday travel season to avoid potential delays.
 For additional information, required documents or to schedule an appointment, visit NJMVC.gov .

 Jay Edwards 
 Born and raised in Northwest NJ, Jay has a degree in Communications and has had a life-long interest in local radio and various styles of music. Jay has held numerous jobs over the years such as stunt car driver, bartender, voice-over artist, traffic reporter (award winning), NY Yankee maintenance crewmember and peanut farm worker. His hobbies include mountain climbing, snowmobiling, cooking, performing stand-up comedy and he is an avid squirrel watcher. Jay has been a guest on America’s Morning Headquarters,program on The Weather Channel, and was interviewed by Sam Champion.
